title: Amyraut: faith's subject is intellect beyond controversy
source_text: II. Praesertim vero istud, tanquam rem certam atque exploratam, affirmat Moses Amyraldus, Thesibus de Fide, parte 1. Thesi 15. & seqq. Subjectum, inquit, cui habitus fidei innascitur, atque inhaeret, facultatem eam esse quae in homine intellectus appellatur, debet esse extra controversiam apud omnes, qui saltem rem istam considerant non omnino oscitanter. Nempe, cum habere fidem nihil aliud sit quam credere, credere autem sit esse persuasum de veritate alicujus rei, fieri nequit quin fides pertineat ad intellectum. Nam & veritas est objectum intellectus; & persuasio non fit aliter, quam admittendo, aut introducendo in intellectum eas rationes, eaque argumenta, quibus unaquaeque res sese veram esse demonstret.
pass_a_gloss: Especially Moses Amyraut affirms this as a certain and settled matter in Theses on Faith, part 1, thesis 15 and following. The subject, he says, in which the habit of faith is born and inheres — that faculty which in man is called intellect — ought to be beyond controversy among all who consider the matter at all carefully. For since to have faith is nothing other than to believe, and to believe is to be persuaded of the truth of some thing, it cannot be that faith does not belong to the intellect. For truth is the object of the intellect; and persuasion does not happen otherwise than by admitting or introducing into the intellect those reasons and arguments by which each thing shows itself to be true.
pass_b_english: Amyraut (Theses de Fide 1.15ff) treats intellect as faith's seat beyond serious dispute.
To have faith = to believe = to be persuaded of truth; persuasion enters by reasons into the intellect.
